claims.text: The nanoparticles are initially solid, single-phase, equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu with a uniform elemental distribution and fully crystalline interior.
The initial nanoparticles are approximately 5 nm in diameter.
The bulk FeNiCrCoCu HEA melting point is approximately 1600 K.
Cu is the lowest-melting-point element in the FeNiCrCoCu system.
Heating causes Cu atoms to diffuse and accumulate at the nanoparticle surface.
Surface Cu enrichment governs the onset and progression of premelting and melting.
Surface-segregated Cu lowers the local surface melting temperature.
Cu accumulation lowers the local melting enthalpy.
Cu enrichment nucleates a subnanometer liquid-like surface shell before the core melts.
The liquid-like surface layer deepens and advances inward as temperature increases.
Premelting will begin 50–150 K below the bulk HEA melting point.
At the premelting temperature, the surface Cu concentration will increase by 10–30 at.%.
A disordered, liquid-like surface layer a few angstroms thick will appear before core collapse.
The proposed mechanism applies to equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles 3–10 nm in diameter under UHV at heating rates no greater than 100 K/s.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to particles larger than 20 nm or to particles heated in reactive atmospheres.
A conformal oxide or ligand shell can inhibit Cu surface segregation.
The controlled comparison consists of uniform particles and shell-treated particles subjected to the same 10 K/s in situ TEM heating protocol.
Premelting at the same temperature in both sets, accompanied by neither measurable Cu enrichment nor a distinct surface liquid layer, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline says the nanoparticles show no detectable disorder or phase change below the bulk melting point, whereas the prediction places premelting and surface disorder 50–150 K below that point. This is inconsistent unless 'baseline' is intended only as the unheated starting state.

The stated conditions exclude surface-active adsorbates, but the proposed inhibited-segregation comparison introduces an oxide or ligand shell that changes the surface environment and may itself affect melting.
The intervention calls for heating above an approximately 1600 K bulk melting point, while the falsification experiment ramps only to 1600 K, which may not reach the specified above-melting regime.
